subject: anatomy
title: Arm, cubital fossa and elbow joint

steps.tx: The **arm** has two compartments separated by the medial and lateral intermuscular septa. The anterior compartment holds the **biceps brachii**, **brachialis** and **coracobrachialis**, all supplied by the **musculocutaneous nerve**. The posterior compartment holds the triceps and is supplied by the radial nerve. Remember this split when answering nerve-supply questions.
steps.say: The arm has two compartments separated by the medial and lateral intermuscular septa. steps.tx: The **cubital fossa** is a triangular hollow in front of the elbow. Its boundaries are the medial border of brachioradialis laterally, the lateral border of pronator teres medially, and an imaginary line joining the two epicondyles as the base. The floor is brachialis above and supinator below. The fossa is a key site for venepuncture.

vis.alt: Right cubital fossa drawn as an inverted triangle: base is the line between the humeral epicondyles, lateral border brachioradialis, medial border pronator teres. Contents from medial to lateral are median nerve, brachial artery, biceps tendon, and radial nerve.
vis.caption: Contents from medial to lateral: median nerve, brachial artery, biceps tendon, radial nerve.

steps.tx: The **median cubital vein** lies superficial to the **bicipital aponeurosis**, which separates it from the deeper brachial artery and median nerve. This is why the vein is preferred for blood sampling and intravenous access. The **cephalic vein** is the paraxial vein and drains into the axillary vein, while the basilic vein is postaxial.

vis.alt: Layered cross-section at the front of the elbow: skin, superficial fascia with the median cubital vein, bicipital aponeurosis, then the brachial artery and median nerve deep to the aponeurosis.
vis.caption: The bicipital aponeurosis is a safety layer between the median cubital vein and the brachial artery and median nerve.

steps.tx: The **elbow joint** is a hinge-type articulation built from three parts: the humeroulnar, humeroradial and proximal radioulnar joints. The first two handle bending and straightening, while the radioulnar component lets the forearm turn palm up and palm down. Clinically, the **carrying angle** is a mild outward tilt of the forearm, and **posterior dislocation** is the commonest form of dislocation at this joint.
